extracted.intended_audience: readers of travelogues, explorers, and mariners (19th-century exploration/natural_history)
extracted.subtask_description: A chapter of a 19th-century ship-based exploration travelogue combining nautical surveying, natural-history observation, route recommendations, and commentary on colonial practice. The page exemplifies how to report observations from voyages for both scientific and practical audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide precise geographical coordinates and measurements
rubrics_metrics.description: Record exact latitudes, longitudes, distances, depths, heights, and compass bearings when describing places and features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text repeatedly gives precise positions and measures (e.g., 'latitude 38 degrees 20 minutes 45 seconds South and longitude 9 degrees 36 minutes 22 seconds West of Sydney'; depths 'in 16 fathoms', 'anchorage was in 7 fathoms'; hill height 'nine hundred and ten feet high'). Use chronometric and triangulation observations and note discrepancies between observers ('the longitude of Sydney... ranges between 151 degrees 12 minutes 0 seconds and 151 degrees 17 minutes 0 seconds').

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer practical navigational advice and hazard warnings
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly identify hazards, safe channels, anchorages, tidal streams and recommended tracks for ships; warn where charts are inaccurate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: mark reefs and sunken rocks (Beagle's Reef, Endeavour Reef), advise 'ships should not pass' between certain marks, give tide sets and timings ('tides... set rather across the channel South-West by South and North-East by North'), and note chart errors ('this part of the coast is laid down ten miles too much to the eastward of Sydney'). Provide leading marks and local rules for entering inlets ('get them on within a mile of the island').

rubrics_metrics.name: Include meteorological and sea-condition observations
rubrics_metrics.description: Report wind directions, barometer readings, fogs, squalls, and their evolution to contextualize voyages and explain navigational decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The narrative links weather to events and decisions (e.g., detailed account of atmospheric changes with barometer values: 'barometer... stood at 29.57', descriptions of calm, fog, gusts, squalls, and consequent sailing performance). Record prevailing winds and their effect on anchorage choice and surveys.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommend exploration routes with clear rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: When proposing routes of inland exploration, state the proposed point of departure, logistical considerations, and reasons (distance, morale, economy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authoritative recommendations include: prefer shortest route to the centre ('the head of the Albert River... is unquestionably the best point of departure'), avoid protracted expeditions to prevent despondency, and logistical suggestions (use camels with water-skins, procure them in the Gulf of Cutch, schedule with monsoons). Discuss alternatives and justify choices with distance comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document natural-history, soil, and geology with examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe flora, fauna, soil quality, rock types and useful agricultural notes to inform settlement and scientific understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Passages note soil fertility ('an acre is capable of feeding one sheep'), vegetation types (stringybark, eucalypti, casuarinas), rock formations ('limestone, ferruginous sandstone, and trap', 'trappean'), and fauna (swans, geese, rabbits). Include observations about water sources and peculiar features (salt stream in island interior).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess and critique colonial land and settlement practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate governmental land policies and their effects on pioneers, recommending remedies when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author criticises systems like the 'Special Survey system' that favour large purchasers over squatters, documents individual grievances (Mr. Henty forced to bid against public for land he improved), and suggests practical remedies ('squatter ought to be allowed to purchase the land he occupies by private contract from government; or that an allowance should be made him, equivalent to his improvements').

rubrics_metrics.name: Propose infrastructure and resource-use solutions for remote regions
rubrics_metrics.description: Make pragmatic recommendations for lighthouses, settlements, convict employment, and provisioning to improve safety and sustainability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: recommend lighthouse locations (Lighthouse Hill, Montague Island, Point Perpendicular), suggest employing convicts in island cultivation to supply prisons ('a small party of convicts might be kept here and advantageously employed'), and propose dispersal of convicts to effect moral improvement and supply foodstuffs for Tasmania.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use vivid narrative and personal experience to convey danger and context
rubrics_metrics.description: When describing perilous situations or significant events, employ vivid sensory detail and personal perspective to communicate urgency and moral/emotional stakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The account of the Beagle narrowly escaping rocks uses evocative language and metaphor ('careering over the waves like the misty spectre in a storm', 'our hearts sickened within at the thought that our little bark... might be left to whiten a foreign shore'). Such narrative techniques make technical incidents engaging and memorable while also documenting events.
